did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, is described as having great wealth and honor, and he was also related by marriage to Ahab, king of Israel.
Did you know? Although Jehoshaphat agreed to join Ahab in battle, he first asked to seek the word of the Lord, emphasizing the importance of prophetic guidance before taking military action.
Did you know? Ahab gathered four hundred prophets, and they all unanimously answered that the army should go to war at Ramoth-gilead and that the king would be granted victory.
Did you know? Ahab admitted that there was another prophet, Micaiah son of Imlah, but said he hated him because his prophecies never foretold anything good for him, only disaster.
Did you know? Micaiah declared in advance that he would not tailor his words to the majority opinion, but would say only what God commanded him to say.

Did you know? In his vision, Micaiah saw the Lord seated on his throne, with all the host of heaven standing at his right and left; this vision presents earthly events as part of an unfolding directed by the Lord.
Did you know? After Micaiah delivered his prophecy, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah struck him on the cheek and challenged the source of the spirit of the Lord speaking through him.
Did you know? Micaiah did not retract his words even after he was sentenced to harsh imprisonment, saying that if Ahab returned safely, then the Lord had not spoken through him.
Did you know? Ahab disguised himself before the battle, while Jehoshaphat remained dressed in royal robes; in this way, they tried to conceal Ahab’s identity while leaving Jehoshaphat exposed.

Did you know? An arrow shot at random struck Ahab where the sections of his armor joined together. He was wounded and died at sunset, although he continued standing in his chariot throughout the battle.
